title: How IIT Kanpur Graduate Satish Kumar Kaura Built Samtel Into a Rs 1,200-Crore Electronics Empire
excerpt: From manufacturing TV picture tubes in a Ghaziabad factory to supplying cockpit displays for fighter jets worldwide, Padma Shri awardee Satish Kumar Kaura's five-decade journey with the Samtel Group traces the arc of Indian manufacturing ambition.
body:
• IIT Kanpur alumnus Satish Kumar Kaura founded the Samtel Group in 1973 after returning from North America, starting with television picture tube manufacturing
  • The group grew into a Rs 1,200-crore conglomerate spanning consumer electronics, defence avionics, and railway systems across nine factories
  • Samtel supplies cockpit displays for Indian Air Force Su-30MKI fighter jets and around 2,000 commercial aircraft in the United States
  • Kaura received the Padma Shri in 2004 and was the first recipient of IIT Kanpur's Distinguished Alumnus Award

When Satish Kumar Kaura graduated from the Indian Institute of Technology, Kanpur, with a degree in electrical engineering in 1966, India's electronics manufacturing sector barely existed. Six decades later, the company he built from a single factory has grown into a multi-business conglomerate with combined revenues exceeding Rs 1,200 crore — a trajectory that mirrors India's own evolution from import dependence to indigenous manufacturing.

From Canada to Ghaziabad

After completing his BTech at IIT Kanpur, Kaura moved to Canada and earned a master's degree in electronics from Carleton University. He gained work experience in North America before making a decision that would shape his career: returning to India in 1973 to start manufacturing.

His first venture was Teletube Electronics Limited, a small unit in Ghaziabad that produced black-and-white television picture tubes for a market that relied almost entirely on imports. When colour television arrived in India during the 1982 Asian Games, Kaura pivoted to colour picture tubes, establishing Samtel Color Limited in 1986 with technical collaborations with Japan's Sumitomo Corporation and Mitsubishi Electric. The operation eventually reached an installed capacity of 10 million picture tubes per year, making it the largest colour picture tube manufacturer in the country and the biggest exporter in the segment.

Pivoting to Defence and Avionics

By the early 2000s, flatscreen panels were displacing conventional TV tubes. Rather than fight a losing battle against obsolescence, Kaura steered Samtel toward a high-value market that was just opening up: defence electronics.

"We are not into transfer of technology or build to print. We are developing our own products for the global market."

— Puneet Kaura, MD and CEO, Samtel Avionics

The pivot was strategic. The government of Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee had begun opening India's defence sector to private manufacturers, and Samtel partnered with the Defence Research and Development Organisation to develop India's first indigenous cockpit display. This led to a joint venture with Hindustan Aeronautics Limited in 2006, forming Samtel HAL Display Systems to manufacture electronic displays for military aircraft. In 2010, Samtel formed another joint venture with French multinational Thales Group to produce Helmet-Mounted Sight and Display Systems.

The results were significant. Samtel has supplied over 1,500 units of Multifunction Displays for the Su-30MKI, cockpit systems for the Light Combat Helicopter and Advanced Light Helicopter, and displays now installed in Malaysian Air Force Su-30s and approximately 2,000 commercial civilian aircraft in the United States.

A Group Built on Reinvention

Today, the Samtel Group encompasses multiple companies. Samtel Avionics, led by Kaura's son Puneet Kaura as Managing Director and CEO, handles the defence and aerospace business. Samtel Engineering and Sourcing Solutions, established in 1983, provides mechanical design and engineering services to global customers. Samtel Glass Limited manufactures critical glass components for display manufacturing. The group operates nine factories across India and Germany, employing thousands of workers.

In recent years, the group has expanded into railway electronics, supplying driver display units and passenger information systems to major propulsion manufacturers including Alstom, Crompton Greaves, and Siemens — tapping into India's massive rail modernisation push.

Recognition and Legacy

Kaura's contributions have earned him the Padma Shri in 2004 for distinguished service in science and engineering. He was the first recipient of IIT Kanpur's Distinguished Alumnus Award in 1989, and has received the Special Recognition Award from the Society for Information Display and the Electronics Man of the Year award. He has served on the board of ICICI Group, as president of the Confederation of Indian Industry's Northern Chapter, and as a member of the DRDO Review Committee and the Prime Minister's Scientific Advisory Council.

Puneet Kaura was named by Aviation Week as one of the top 40 leaders under 40 in the global aerospace and defence industry — the only Indian to make that list.

What Comes Next

As India pushes for greater self-reliance in defence manufacturing and the government seeks indigenous avionics systems, the Samtel Group is exploring AI-integrated avionics, sensor technologies for Indian Navy ships and Army helicopters, and advanced military vehicle displays for a US-based OEM. Kaura also established the Modern Public School in Bhiwadi, Rajasthan, in 1986, which has grown to a 5,000-student institution — a quieter legacy alongside the industrial one.

From a single factory making TV tubes to a conglomerate that puts displays in fighter jet cockpits, Kaura's journey is a case study in how Indian engineering talent, patient capital, and willingness to reinvent can build manufacturing enterprises that compete globally.
